question: How can linear models be extended to nonlinear functions by augmenting inputs with basis expansions, and how is the resulting flexibility controlled by restriction, selection or regularization?
contributions: Linear basis expansions f(X)=sum beta_m h_m(X) (5.1) with three complexity controls: restriction, selection, regularization
Piecewise polynomials, regression splines, natural cubic splines, B-splines
Smoothing splines with effective degrees of freedom trace(S_lambda), smoother matrix, Reinsch form, CV by the leave-one-out shortcut
Nonparametric logistic regression, tensor-product and thin-plate splines
RKHS view of regularization (kernel property), Gaussian RBF, penalized polynomial regression
Wavelet bases with SURE soft-threshold shrinkage

results.claim: Restricting phoneme logistic-regression coefficients to a smooth natural-spline expansion (M=12) cuts test error from 0.255 (raw 256 inputs) to 0.158.
results.setup: Phoneme 'aa' vs 'ao', 256 log-periodogram inputs, training sample 1000 drawn from 695 aa and 1022 ao; linear logistic regression; smooth coefficient beta=H theta, M=12 natural cubic spline basis, knots uniform over 1..256
results.table: Section 5.2.3 table, row Test error, column Regularized (0.158; raw 0.255)

results.claim: Raw (unrestricted) phoneme logistic regression fits training data far better than the smooth one but generalises worse: training error 0.080 raw vs 0.185 regularized.
results.table: Section 5.2.3 table, row Training error, column Raw (0.080; regularized 0.185)

results.claim: Natural cubic spline with K knots needs only K basis functions; the linear-beyond-boundary constraint frees four degrees of freedom to spend on interior knots.
results.setup: 1-D natural cubic spline vs cubic spline, Fig 5.3 (50 points from U[0,1], six df splines, knots at 0.33/0.66 vs boundary 0.1/0.9 plus four interior)
results.quote: A natural cubic spline with K knots is represented by K basis functions.

results.claim: A smoothing spline's effective degrees of freedom is defined as the trace of the smoother matrix, df_lambda = trace(S_lambda).
results.setup: Smoothing spline, linear smoother f-hat = S_lambda y
results.note: Definition (5.16); quote not recorded, value null

results.claim: Bone-density smoothing splines for males and females were fit with df=12, which corresponds numerically to lambda about 0.00022.
results.setup: Relative change in spinal BMD vs age in adolescents, separate smoothing spline per sex, df_lambda=12 solved from trace(S_lambda)=12

results.claim: Leave-one-out CV for a linear smoother is computed from one fit: CV = sum ((y_i - f_i)/(1 - S_lambda(i,i)))^2, so no refits are needed.
results.setup: Smoothing spline with smoother matrix S_lambda, eq 5.26-5.27
results.quote: which can (remarkably) be computed for each value of λ from the original ﬁtted values and the diagonal elements Sλ(i, i) of Sλ

results.claim: In the bias-variance simulation, EPE is minimised near df=9 for the true function sin(12(x+0.2))/(x+0.2); df=5 underfits (narrow bands, high bias) and df=15 is wiggly.
results.setup: Y=f(X)+eps, X~U[0,1], eps~N(0,1), N=100, smoothing spline, EPE and N-fold CV curves (single realisation shown)
results.quote: The blue points in the top left panel of Figure 5.9 suggest that dfλ = 9 is spot on!

results.claim: Leave-one-out CV curve is approximately unbiased for EPE overall, though in the example the whole CV curve lies above the EPE curve.
results.quote: overall the CV curve is approximately unbiased as an estimate of the EPE curve

results.claim: Additive natural-spline logistic regression on the Chapter 2 simulation (4 df per coordinate, total df 7) has test error 0.28 against Bayes error 0.21.
results.setup: Simulated two-class mixture example of Fig 2.1; logit model with natural splines in each of two coordinates; training error 0.23
results.note: Training error 0.23 and Bayes 0.21; the tensor-product panel prints 0.230, 0.282 and 0.210

results.claim: Tensor-product natural-spline basis (4x4 = 16 df) gives test error 0.282, no better than the additive 7-df model (0.28), and adds spurious structure at the boundary.
results.setup: Same simulation; tensor product of natural spline bases, total df 16

results.claim: A stepwise-deleted natural-spline logistic model for South African heart disease reaches deviance 458.09 and AIC 502.09 with terms sbp, tobacco, ldl, famhist, obesity, age.
results.setup: Natural splines, 4 basis functions per continuous term (famhist a single dummy); backward deletion by group using AIC

results.claim: Deleting famhist raises AIC from 502.09 to 521.44 (LRT 21.356, 1 df); deleting age raises it to 517.86 (LRT 23.768, 4 df); deleting sbp or obesity changes AIC by only about 1 (503.16, 502.24).
Gaussian-kernel ridge regression on 200 points has an effective feature-space dimension of about 12 although the implicit space is infinite; eigenvalues beyond the 30th are effectively zero.
results.setup: Radial kernel nu=1, first coordinate of mixture data, 200x200 kernel matrix, Fig 5.14-5.15
results.quote: leaving an eﬀective dimension of about 12 in this case

results.claim: Soft-threshold wavelet shrinkage solves an L1 criterion in closed form for an orthonormal basis: theta_j = sign(y*_j)(|y*_j| - lambda)+, with lambda = sigma sqrt(2 log N).
results.setup: Orthonormal wavelet basis W, N=2^J uniformly spaced points, y* = W^T y; noise sd sigma estimated from data
results.quote: A simple choice for λ is λ = σ√2 log N

results.claim: The wavelet transform costs O(N) (faster than FFT's N log N); smoothing-spline fitting with B-splines is O(N) via a banded Cholesky; thin-plate splines cost O(N^3), or O(NK^2+K^3) with K knots.
results.quote: can be obtained in O(N) computations, which is even faster than the N log(N) of the fast Fourier transform (FFT)

limits: Splines and wavelets are developed mainly in one dimension; the basis grows exponentially with dimension (tensor products) and thin-plate splines cost O(N^3) (Sec 5.7).
Natural splines trade extra bias near the boundaries for lower variance (Sec 5.2.1).
Knot placement/number for regression splines is combinatorially hard; the chapter defers to MARS (Ch 9) (Sec 5.5).
Smoothing-parameter selection is only sketched (CV, GCV, Cp are pointed to Chapter 7); the bias-variance figure is a single realisation (Sec 5.5.2).
Wavelet fit adds unnecessary wiggles for smooth functions with high noise (variance price for adaptivity) (Sec 5.9.2, Fig 5.19).
Heart-disease nonlinearities at low obesity/sbp are attributed to retrospective data, not a causal effect (Sec 5.2.2).
The experiments report single splits and no seeds; no code is given (S-PLUS/R function names only). Dated: S-PLUS waveshrink, bs()/smooth.spline defaults of 2009.
practices: Use basis expansions h_m(X) and then fit a linear model in the derived features; fitting proceeds as before (Sec 5.1).
Avoid global polynomials: they flap in remote regions; use piecewise polynomials/splines (Sec 5.1).
Cubic splines are the usual choice; orders M=1, 2, 4 are the most used; seldom a reason to go beyond cubic (Sec 5.2).
Parameterise a regression spline by df and let data quantiles place knots, e.g. bs(x, df=7) puts interior knots at 20/40/60/80th percentiles (Sec 5.2).
Prefer the B-spline basis to truncated powers numerically (Sec 5.2, Appendix).
Use natural cubic splines when boundary variance matters; spend freed df on interior knots (Sec 5.2.1).
Drop spline terms as groups (all basis columns of a variable together) in stepwise selection, using AIC (Sec 5.2.2).

Smooth high-dimensional ordered features (signals) by projecting x*=H^T x onto a spline basis before a learner; domain-derived preprocessing often improves any learner, e.g. wavelets then a neural net (Sec 5.2.3).
Specify smoothers by effective df = trace(S) to compare methods uniformly and fit by F-tests or residual plots (Sec 5.5.1).
Choose lambda by cross-validation; for linear smoothers use the leave-one-out shortcut with S(i,i) (Sec 5.5.2).
For thin-plate splines use a lattice of knots inside the convex hull of the data (Sec 5.7).
For signals with isolated spikes use wavelet soft-threshold shrinkage (lambda = sigma sqrt(2 log N)); for smooth truths smoothing splines are better (Sec 5.9.2).
